medical.title: AI-designed proteins outperform existing CAR T designs against BCMA tumors in mice
medical.summary: CAR T cell therapy, which involves genetically modifying a patient's own immune cells to fight cancer, is a technique that has shown great promise, especially against blood cancers. But currently, only about 4% of patients with advanced or metastatic cancer in the United States are candidates for CAR T therapy, and closer to 3% will actually benefit, according to one recent analysis.

medical.title: Blocking a protein may reduce buildup of harmful aging cells
medical.summary: A team led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University investigators has identified a protein that may hide aging cells from the body's immune system, allowing them to build up and contribute to age-related health problems.

medical.title: Autism linked to 14-year gap in life expectancy
medical.summary: People with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in the United States face a 14-year deficit in life expectancy, according to a new study by researchers at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and University of Colorado Anschutz. The study provides one of the first large-scale estimates of age-specific death rates and life expectancy among people with ASD. The findings are published in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Starting diabetes medicine sooner after kidney injury may protect kidneys
medical.summary: A study of adults with type 2 diabetes recovering from dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury found that patients who began an SGLT-2 inhibitor within 30 days of hospital discharge had fewer serious kidney events than those who started the medicine 31 to 90 days after discharge. The research, led by National Taiwan University Hospital and published in JAMA Network Open, examines an important question about treatment during kidney recovery.

medical.title: Blood protein analysis suggests a lung disease drug could be fighting aging at the same time
medical.summary: In 2025, Insilico Medicine developed an experimental drug called rentosertib as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a severe age-related lung disease. The drug works by inhibiting the protein TNIK, which is involved in both scar tissue formation in the lungs and fundamental hallmarks of biological aging. The researchers wondered whether rentosertib could serve as a dual-purpose drug that treats aging-related diseases and may also affect the aging process itself.

medical.title: From autism to Alzheimer's: Membrane transporters open new avenues for treating brain disorders
medical.summary: Solute carriers (SLCs) are specialized transport proteins that control the movement of nutrients, ions and neurotransmitters across cell membranes and are essential for brain metabolism and neuronal communication. While some SLCs have been targeted successfully by drugs for decades, most of this large protein family remains therapeutically unexplored.

medical.title: From sadness to relief: How families cope with assisted dying grief
medical.summary: New research exploring how people cope when a family member chooses assisted dying highlights the "roller coaster" of emotions they often experience.

medical.title: New Mathematical model estimates curable window for fast-growing lung tumors
medical.summary: Detecting lung cancer early is critical to a patient's survival, but how early is early enough? Florida International University math professor and researcher Deborah Goldwasser is uncovering new findings that could identify the mathematical tipping point between curable and terminal cancer. Her work could change how doctors determine the best timing for lung cancer screening by correcting statistical biases that may be overestimating the window for curing aggressive cancers.

medical.title: Child cancer groups call for concerted action
medical.summary: It's one of the cruelest ironies in health and medicine. Pediatric sarcomas are among the rarest yet most aggressive forms of childhood cancer and some of the hardest to cure. Whereas many adult cancers are now treatable with new therapeutic strategies, such as immunotherapies, pediatric sarcomas have not seen nearly as many advances. Survival rates have remained largely unchanged for decades.

medical.title: New survey highlights persistent cancer medication shortages across United States
medical.summary: The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN)—an alliance of leading cancer centers—has published updated data on the current impact of generic cancer medication shortages in the United States. The data come from survey responses from pharmacy directors and other clinical and administrative leaders at NCCN Member Institutions from late August. According to the results, 100% of responding cancer centers are experiencing a shortage of at least one anticancer agent, with more than 20% of centers currently experiencing shortages of five or more different medications.

medical.title: Popular weight-loss drug could change how doctors treat sleep apnea
medical.summary: One in eight people worldwide does not get an uninterrupted night's sleep because of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This sleep disorder causes people to wake up suddenly when a blockage or narrowing in the upper airway prevents air from flowing properly through the windpipe. These repeated interruptions can leave a person exhausted, even after what's technically a full night's sleep. Obesity is a contributing factor to this sleep disorder, so researchers reviewed existing literature to see how GLP-1 receptor agonist medications, a class of weight-loss and diabetes drugs, can be used to treat OSA.

science.title: Fossil flowers of ancient lianas preserved in amber reveal the evolution of tropical rainforests
science.summary: Tiny flowers trapped in amber around 15 million years ago are offering scientists a rare glimpse into the plant life of a tropical rainforest in what is now Southeast China. Researchers have studied two exceptionally well-preserved fossil flowers from the Zhangpu flora.

science.title: Report maps pathways for accelerating environmental solutions through positive tipping points
science.summary: New research from The Earthshot Prize and the University of Exeter's Green Futures Solutions team, published today, reveals 51 environmental solutions that can trigger rapid, transformative change to repair our planet within the next five years. After a northern summer of extreme heat and fire, and as the world prepares for an unprecedented El Niño, the research provides a new, unifying agenda for positive action.

science.title: Indonesia rescues six orangutans from fires in a week
science.summary: Six orangutans, including two nursing infants, have been rescued from fires raging on Borneo in the past week, Indonesian authorities and rescuers said Thursday, bringing the total to 15 in a month.

science.title: Peer-led computing camps engage children, study finds
science.summary: High school student Khushi Kharuna creates and leads coding and artificial intelligence (AI) summer camps for K–12 students in her community outside Philadelphia. Priya Kumar, PNC Technologies Career Development Professor in Penn State's College of Information Sciences and Technology (IST), studies how young people navigate the digital world. Their shared interests led to a research collaboration exploring a youth-led STEM learning model that puts children's voices at the center of the learning experience.

science.title: A fossil feather preserved inside dinosaur poop could help explain why birds survived the mass extinction
science.summary: About 66 million years ago, a dinosaur—maybe a T. rex or a Nanotyrannus—ate a bird. The record of that meal, in the form of fossilized poop, has survived to today, preserving the best example of a feather ever found from the age of dinosaurs. By studying this feather, scientists reported in a new study in the journal Current Biology, researchers have found clues that help explain why birds are the only group of dinosaurs that survived the mass extinction 66 million years ago.

science.title: Scientists want to 3D print houses on Mars with the help of yeast
science.summary: Mars is a terrible place to build a house. It's bitterly cold, blasted by radiation and a near vacuum. Not to mention that the building materials, even for a modest shelter, could spend months hurtling through space before construction begins.

science.title: BepiColombo measures Mercury's particle bombardment up close
science.summary: The joint BepiColombo mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is settling into orbit around Mercury after an eight-year journey. In early September, BepiColombo's two orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, separated from the transfer module. The orbiters will enter Mercury's orbit in November and separate from each other in December.

science.title: Simple farming changes boost wheat yields in drought-prone areas
science.summary: In drought-prone regions of Ethiopia, growing more food could start with something as simple as keeping more rainwater in the ground.

science.title: Asteroid Ryugu's dust reveals nitrogen's slow concentration into complex molecules
science.summary: Nitrogen is a key ingredient in the biomolecules that form the building blocks of life. Yet as an unbonded gas, it is far more likely to drift into space than to lock itself into solid compounds, making it difficult for astronomers to trace its journey to Earth in the distant past.

science.title: Chinese cave traces Denisovan hunting and adaptation across 120,000 years
science.summary: An ancient cave in southwestern China has revealed new evidence about how Denisovans—an ancient human relative—lived, survived and adapted over more than 100,000 years.

science.title: Spinons may help electrons pair along stripes in some superconductors
science.summary: Superconductors are materials that carry electricity with zero resistance below specific temperatures. Many of these materials become superconducting at very low temperatures, yet some enter superconducting phases at higher temperatures.

science.title: Hungry scent detection dogs more likely to 'cry wolf'
science.summary: Dogs trained in scent detection may be better at sniffing out the right smell after breakfast, with new research finding hungry dogs working for treats are more likely to falsely identify the wrong scent. The study, led by researchers from the University of Waikato and Adelaide University, explored how meal timing affected dogs' accuracy in detecting target scents.

science.title: 'Fingerprints' inside the sun could reveal if it once swallowed a planet
science.summary: It is thought the sun may have engulfed a super-Earth-sized planet early in its history. Now, a new study has gone a step further, suggesting that such an event may have left behind detectable clues inside the sun that could still be visible today.

science.title: Australia's reading and math results are at an 'all‑time low'—but there's more to the story
science.summary: Results from the latest international test of 15-year-olds have prompted another round of headlines suggesting there are serious problems with Australia's academic results.

science.title: Mercury is shrinking more than we thought
science.summary: Mercury's surface is riddled with wrinkles, evidence of a once-larger planet that has shrunk over time. A new study finds that Mercury may have contracted 10% to 30% more than previously thought—a loss of nearly 12 miles (19 kilometers) of total diameter since the planet formed—due to debris from impact craters obscuring signs of the planet's shrinking.

science.title: 'Peculiar' new species of Jurassic squid found in Wyoming
science.summary: A "peculiar" new species of Jurassic squid-like animal has been unearthed in Wyoming, U.S., following the discovery of two exceptionally rare fossils dating to around 160 million years ago.

science.title: Rib contouring highlights social media's role in reshaping body ideals and surgical interest
science.summary: Rib contouring—a cosmetic procedure aimed at creating a smaller, more defined waist—is one of the newer appearance trends on social media. Influencers are sharing their experiences online, bringing a procedure many of us had probably never heard of into our social media feeds.

science.title: Scavenging linked to virus variety in wild birds
science.summary: The scavenging behavior of many wild birds plays an important role in the type, number and variety of viruses they have, a new University of Otago–Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka-led study has found.

science.title: A galaxy with almost no stars? New Cloud-9 observations strengthen the case
science.summary: Astronomers have taken one of the deepest looks yet at Cloud-9, a candidate "dark galaxy," and found no trace of stars. The paper outlining this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 21.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: Tiny flowers trapped in amber around 15 million years ago are offering scientists a rare glimpse into the plant life of a tropical rainforest in what is now Southeast China. Researchers have studied two exceptionally well-preserved fossil flowers from the Zhangpu flora.

mix_items.summary: CAR T cell therapy, which involves genetically modifying a patient's own immune cells to fight cancer, is a technique that has shown great promise, especially against blood cancers. But currently, only about 4% of patients with advanced or metastatic cancer in the United States are candidates for CAR T therapy, and closer to 3% will actually benefit, according to one recent analysis.

mix_items.title: Report maps pathways for accelerating environmental solutions through positive tipping points
mix_items.summary: New research from The Earthshot Prize and the University of Exeter's Green Futures Solutions team, published today, reveals 51 environmental solutions that can trigger rapid, transformative change to repair our planet within the next five years. After a northern summer of extreme heat and fire, and as the world prepares for an unprecedented El Niño, the research provides a new, unifying agenda for positive action.

mix_items.title: Indonesia rescues six orangutans from fires in a week
mix_items.summary: Six orangutans, including two nursing infants, have been rescued from fires raging on Borneo in the past week, Indonesian authorities and rescuers said Thursday, bringing the total to 15 in a month.

mix_items.title: Blocking a protein may reduce buildup of harmful aging cells
mix_items.summary: A team led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University investigators has identified a protein that may hide aging cells from the body's immune system, allowing them to build up and contribute to age-related health problems.

mix_items.title: Peer-led computing camps engage children, study finds
mix_items.summary: High school student Khushi Kharuna creates and leads coding and artificial intelligence (AI) summer camps for K–12 students in her community outside Philadelphia. Priya Kumar, PNC Technologies Career Development Professor in Penn State's College of Information Sciences and Technology (IST), studies how young people navigate the digital world. Their shared interests led to a research collaboration exploring a youth-led STEM learning model that puts children's voices at the center of the learning experience.

mix_items.title: Autism linked to 14-year gap in life expectancy
mix_items.summary: People with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in the United States face a 14-year deficit in life expectancy, according to a new study by researchers at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and University of Colorado Anschutz. The study provides one of the first large-scale estimates of age-specific death rates and life expectancy among people with ASD. The findings are published in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: A fossil feather preserved inside dinosaur poop could help explain why birds survived the mass extinction
mix_items.summary: About 66 million years ago, a dinosaur—maybe a T. rex or a Nanotyrannus—ate a bird. The record of that meal, in the form of fossilized poop, has survived to today, preserving the best example of a feather ever found from the age of dinosaurs. By studying this feather, scientists reported in a new study in the journal Current Biology, researchers have found clues that help explain why birds are the only group of dinosaurs that survived the mass extinction 66 million years ago.

mix_items.title: Scientists want to 3D print houses on Mars with the help of yeast
mix_items.summary: Mars is a terrible place to build a house. It's bitterly cold, blasted by radiation and a near vacuum. Not to mention that the building materials, even for a modest shelter, could spend months hurtling through space before construction begins.

mix_items.title: BepiColombo measures Mercury's particle bombardment up close
mix_items.summary: The joint BepiColombo mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is settling into orbit around Mercury after an eight-year journey. In early September, BepiColombo's two orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, separated from the transfer module. The orbiters will enter Mercury's orbit in November and separate from each other in December.

mix_items.title: Starting diabetes medicine sooner after kidney injury may protect kidneys
mix_items.summary: A study of adults with type 2 diabetes recovering from dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury found that patients who began an SGLT-2 inhibitor within 30 days of hospital discharge had fewer serious kidney events than those who started the medicine 31 to 90 days after discharge. The research, led by National Taiwan University Hospital and published in JAMA Network Open, examines an important question about treatment during kidney recovery.

mix_items.title: Simple farming changes boost wheat yields in drought-prone areas
mix_items.summary: In drought-prone regions of Ethiopia, growing more food could start with something as simple as keeping more rainwater in the ground.

mix_items.title: Asteroid Ryugu's dust reveals nitrogen's slow concentration into complex molecules
mix_items.summary: Nitrogen is a key ingredient in the biomolecules that form the building blocks of life. Yet as an unbonded gas, it is far more likely to drift into space than to lock itself into solid compounds, making it difficult for astronomers to trace its journey to Earth in the distant past.

mix_items.title: Blood protein analysis suggests a lung disease drug could be fighting aging at the same time
mix_items.summary: In 2025, Insilico Medicine developed an experimental drug called rentosertib as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a severe age-related lung disease. The drug works by inhibiting the protein TNIK, which is involved in both scar tissue formation in the lungs and fundamental hallmarks of biological aging. The researchers wondered whether rentosertib could serve as a dual-purpose drug that treats aging-related diseases and may also affect the aging process itself.

mix_items.title: From autism to Alzheimer's: Membrane transporters open new avenues for treating brain disorders
mix_items.summary: Solute carriers (SLCs) are specialized transport proteins that control the movement of nutrients, ions and neurotransmitters across cell membranes and are essential for brain metabolism and neuronal communication. While some SLCs have been targeted successfully by drugs for decades, most of this large protein family remains therapeutically unexplored.

mix_items.title: Chinese cave traces Denisovan hunting and adaptation across 120,000 years
mix_items.summary: An ancient cave in southwestern China has revealed new evidence about how Denisovans—an ancient human relative—lived, survived and adapted over more than 100,000 years.

mix_items.title: Spinons may help electrons pair along stripes in some superconductors
mix_items.summary: Superconductors are materials that carry electricity with zero resistance below specific temperatures. Many of these materials become superconducting at very low temperatures, yet some enter superconducting phases at higher temperatures.

mix_items.title: From sadness to relief: How families cope with assisted dying grief
mix_items.summary: New research exploring how people cope when a family member chooses assisted dying highlights the "roller coaster" of emotions they often experience.

mix_items.title: New Mathematical model estimates curable window for fast-growing lung tumors
mix_items.summary: Detecting lung cancer early is critical to a patient's survival, but how early is early enough? Florida International University math professor and researcher Deborah Goldwasser is uncovering new findings that could identify the mathematical tipping point between curable and terminal cancer. Her work could change how doctors determine the best timing for lung cancer screening by correcting statistical biases that may be overestimating the window for curing aggressive cancers.

mix_items.title: Hungry scent detection dogs more likely to 'cry wolf'
mix_items.summary: Dogs trained in scent detection may be better at sniffing out the right smell after breakfast, with new research finding hungry dogs working for treats are more likely to falsely identify the wrong scent. The study, led by researchers from the University of Waikato and Adelaide University, explored how meal timing affected dogs' accuracy in detecting target scents.

mix_items.title: Child cancer groups call for concerted action
mix_items.summary: It's one of the cruelest ironies in health and medicine. Pediatric sarcomas are among the rarest yet most aggressive forms of childhood cancer and some of the hardest to cure. Whereas many adult cancers are now treatable with new therapeutic strategies, such as immunotherapies, pediatric sarcomas have not seen nearly as many advances. Survival rates have remained largely unchanged for decades.

mix_items.title: 'Fingerprints' inside the sun could reveal if it once swallowed a planet
mix_items.summary: It is thought the sun may have engulfed a super-Earth-sized planet early in its history. Now, a new study has gone a step further, suggesting that such an event may have left behind detectable clues inside the sun that could still be visible today.

mix_items.title: Australia's reading and math results are at an 'all‑time low'—but there's more to the story
mix_items.summary: Results from the latest international test of 15-year-olds have prompted another round of headlines suggesting there are serious problems with Australia's academic results.

mix_items.title: Mercury is shrinking more than we thought
mix_items.summary: Mercury's surface is riddled with wrinkles, evidence of a once-larger planet that has shrunk over time. A new study finds that Mercury may have contracted 10% to 30% more than previously thought—a loss of nearly 12 miles (19 kilometers) of total diameter since the planet formed—due to debris from impact craters obscuring signs of the planet's shrinking.

mix_items.title: New survey highlights persistent cancer medication shortages across United States
mix_items.summary: The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN)—an alliance of leading cancer centers—has published updated data on the current impact of generic cancer medication shortages in the United States. The data come from survey responses from pharmacy directors and other clinical and administrative leaders at NCCN Member Institutions from late August. According to the results, 100% of responding cancer centers are experiencing a shortage of at least one anticancer agent, with more than 20% of centers currently experiencing shortages of five or more different medications.

mix_items.title: 'Peculiar' new species of Jurassic squid found in Wyoming
mix_items.summary: A "peculiar" new species of Jurassic squid-like animal has been unearthed in Wyoming, U.S., following the discovery of two exceptionally rare fossils dating to around 160 million years ago.

mix_items.title: Popular weight-loss drug could change how doctors treat sleep apnea
mix_items.summary: One in eight people worldwide does not get an uninterrupted night's sleep because of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This sleep disorder causes people to wake up suddenly when a blockage or narrowing in the upper airway prevents air from flowing properly through the windpipe. These repeated interruptions can leave a person exhausted, even after what's technically a full night's sleep. Obesity is a contributing factor to this sleep disorder, so researchers reviewed existing literature to see how GLP-1 receptor agonist medications, a class of weight-loss and diabetes drugs, can be used to treat OSA.

mix_items.title: Rib contouring highlights social media's role in reshaping body ideals and surgical interest
mix_items.summary: Rib contouring—a cosmetic procedure aimed at creating a smaller, more defined waist—is one of the newer appearance trends on social media. Influencers are sharing their experiences online, bringing a procedure many of us had probably never heard of into our social media feeds.

mix_items.title: Scavenging linked to virus variety in wild birds
mix_items.summary: The scavenging behavior of many wild birds plays an important role in the type, number and variety of viruses they have, a new University of Otago–Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka-led study has found.

mix_items.title: A galaxy with almost no stars? New Cloud-9 observations strengthen the case
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have taken one of the deepest looks yet at Cloud-9, a candidate "dark galaxy," and found no trace of stars. The paper outlining this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 21.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

satire_ro.title: E oficial! Ca să punem capăt glumelor cu „anus”, planeta Uranus va fi redenumită Urinus
